title: Origen grants angels only the honor of praise and imitation
source_text: LXIX. Itaque Origenes pulsatus Celsi objectionibus, quasi Christiani summi Dei Ministros, & Angelicas potestates contemnerent, & nullo honore prosequerentur, non alium honorem illis exhibendum esse concedit, quam eum qui consistit in laude & imitatione: Eos, inquit, praedicamus beatos, & bene loquimur de illis, quibus a Deo commissae sunt utilitates hominum, non tamen honorem Deo debitum his reddimus. Saepius jam citato libro adversus Celsum Philosophum octavo. Ac praeterea loco quem supra descripsimus ex libro quinto ejusdem operis, affirmat Angelos, quantum humana natura fert, nobis imitandos esse; idque satis fore ut beati illi Spiritus bene nobis velint, & pro nobis in omnibus satagant: sed nullibi, quod tamen ad ejus scopum maxime fecisset, & calumniam Ethnicorum plenius adhuc retudisset, memorat nos eorum orationes precibus ambire, aut quicquam eorum quae in Ecclesia Romana hodie usitata sunt, in eorum honorem fieri.
pass_a_gloss: And so Origen, struck by the objections of Celsus, as though the Christians despised the Ministers of the supreme God, and the Angelic powers, and followed them with no honor, concedes that no other honor is to be shown to them than that which consists in praise and imitation: Them, he says, we proclaim blessed, and we speak well of those to whom the interests of men have been committed by God, yet we do not render to them the honor owed to God. In the often already cited eighth book against Celsus the Philosopher. And moreover in the place which we described above from the fifth book of the same work, he affirms that the Angels, as far as human nature allows, are to be imitated by us; and that this will be enough for those blessed Spirits to wish us well, and to busy themselves for us in all things: but nowhere, which nevertheless would have served his purpose most, and would have beaten back the calumny of the Heathen still more fully, does he mention that we court their prayers with our prayers, or that anything of those things which are in use today in the Roman Church is done in their honor.
pass_b_english: So Origen, pressed by Celsus's objections that Christians despised the servants of the supreme God and the angelic powers and gave them no honor at all, grants that no other honor is to be given them than the honor that consists in praise and imitation. "We call them blessed," he says, "and we speak well of those to whom God has entrusted the welfare of human beings, yet we do not give them the honor owed to God." (Against Celsus the Philosopher, book 8, cited several times already.)

In the passage from book 5 of the same work quoted above, he also states that we are to imitate the angels as far as human nature allows, and that this will be enough for those blessed spirits to wish us well and to take pains for us in everything. But nowhere does he mention that we solicit their prayers by praying to them, or that any of the things used in the Roman Church today are done in their honor, though that would have served his purpose best and would have refuted the pagan slander even more fully.

lemmas.gloss: to court their prayers with prayers

choices.why: Ambire is canvassing for favor; 'solicit' keeps the image of courting intercession.
